Lesson 0001 • Foundational Theory

PWM & The Evolution of Automotive Control

In modern vehicles, electricity does far more than turn devices simply "on" or "off." It precisely controls the speed of fuel pumps, the cooling rate of radiator fans, and the brightness of instrument clusters. To understand how cars achieve this, we first look at where they started.

The Old Way: Resistor Packs & Dissipated Heat

Before modern computers controlled cars, varying the speed of an electric component (like a cabin blower fan) was done using series resistors. These resistors restrict current flow, dropping the voltage reaching the motor.

The Critical Efficiency Flaw

Resistors control speed by converting unwanted electrical energy into heat. In older cars, resistor packs had to sit inside the ventilation duct so the incoming air could cool them down.

The Modern Way: Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)

Modern vehicles use solid-state transistors (typically MOSFETs) inside the Engine Control Unit. Instead of placing a resistive restriction, the transistor acts as an ultra-fast switch, turning the supply fully ON and fully OFF thousands of times per second. By varying the ratio of "on-time" to "off-time," the ECU controls the average voltage received by the actuator without wasting power as heat.

Key Parameters of a PWM Signal

  1. Duty Cycle: the percentage of time the signal is ON during one cycle.
  2. Period (T): the total time of one complete ON/OFF cycle.
  3. Frequency (f): cycles per second, f = 1 / T, measured in Hz.

Try it

Reduce the Frequency slider to 2–5 Hz and watch the fan pulse and the bulb flicker. In cars, PWM runs between 100 Hz and 20 kHz — fast enough that switching is invisible and motor inertia smooths the speed.
